deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 183 continues a set of German-language notes on Hellenistic Greek history, picking up from the previous page on the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues. The handwriting, layout and content suggest student lecture notes on ancient history (Göttingen style, possibly copied from or kept alongside Gauss's papers), not a mathematical manuscript.

Content, in order:
(1) Antigonus (Gonatas) worked against the Achaeans as far as he could and therefore allied himself with the Aetolians, but he was already too old. The margin gives his death as † 243. He left two sons, Demetrius and Antigonus.
(2) Demetrius II reigned first, 243 to † 233. He also worked against the Achaeans by supporting the tyrants in Greece. He left an under-age son, Philipp.
(3) Antigonus 'II' Doson reigned 233 to † 221. Under him a revolution took place in Sparta.
(4) Agis 'II' tried in 244 to restore the Lycurgan constitution, but was killed in 241 through Leonidas. Leonidas died † 236 and left a son, Cleomenes, who succeeded him and took up Agis's plan again. Cleomenes first gave his own property to the state. In 227 he defeated the Achaeans, who wanted to force Sparta into their league. In 226 he surprised the ephors, killed them and restored the old constitution. Because he could not suppress the opposing party without war, he began a war against the Achaeans.
(5) The Achaeans called in the Macedonians and Doson to help. Doson came in 222. At Sellasia there was a decisive battle; the sentence continues on folio 184.

There are no derivations, formulas or calculations to reconstruct. The only numbers are BC dates.
errors: Not mathematical errors, but historical inaccuracies relative to modern chronology.
Antigonus Gonatas died in 239 BC, not 243.
Antigonus Doson reigned 229–221 BC, not 233–221. He is also normally numbered Antigonus III, not II.
The Spartan reformer is Agis IV, not 'Agis II'.
Leonidas II died c. 235 BC; 236 is close.
Cleomenes III's coup against the ephors is usually dated 227 BC, not 226.
Sellasia is dated 222 BC; some scholars argue for 223. The note's 222 is consistent with the standard date.
These date shifts reflect older chronologies in use around 1800 and are not slips peculiar to the writer.

results.what: Narrative notes on Macedonian and Spartan history c. 244–222 BC: Antigonus Gonatas, Demetrius II, Antigonus Doson, the reforms of Agis IV and Cleomenes III, and the Cleomenean War up to Sellasia.
results.modern_name: Hellenistic political history (Cleomenean War); not mathematics
results.usually_credited_to: Standard ancient-history content (Polybius, Plutarch's Lives of Agis and Cleomenes; 18th–19th c. handbooks such as Heeren's)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains only routine historical lecture notes, with no mathematical content. It is very likely not even in Gauss's hand or of his authorship.

checkable.asserts: Length of Demetrius II's reign according to the notes' dates (10 years; modern 239–229 also gives 10).
Length of Antigonus Doson's reign according to the notes' dates (modern 229–221 gives 8).
Interval between Agis's reform attempt and his death according to the notes.

transcription_corrections: 'Antigonus II Doson' and 'Agis II' are as written in the manuscript; they should not be silently corrected to III and IV.

In 'Diese zogen den Ma-cedoner[?] u ihren[?] Doson zu Hülfe', the words after 'den' are uncertain in the image. The reading may be 'Ma-cedonier' or something similar and should remain marked uncertain.
'Philipp' at the end of line 8 is underlined in the manuscript, as are 'Antigonus II Doson', 'Lycurgische', 'Cleomenes', 'Ephoren', 'Doson' and 'Sellasia'.
The marginal mark at lower right appears to read '& d'' (perhaps a catchword or cross-reference), rather than just '&'.
'Ephoren' is written with an underlined split ('Ep horen') across the pen strokes; the reading 'Ephoren' is correct.
